chunks: "The standard tool is a PLL, a phase-locked loop, used as a frequency multiplier.
You start with a stable, low-frequency reference like a crystal, say 25 megahertz, and the PLL has an oscillator, a VCO, running at the high frequency, with a divide-by-N in the feedback path.
The loop forces the divided-down VCO to line up with the reference, so the VCO runs at N times the reference.
With N equal to 40, that 25 megahertz crystal becomes a 1 gigahertz clock. Why not just buy a gigahertz crystal?
Crystals don't make fundamental frequencies that high with good stability and low cost, and you want one cheap, quiet reference that a programmable PLL can scale to whatever the chip needs.
A PLL also lets software change the clock on the fly. There are other options. A simple frequency doubler can use an XOR of the clock with a delayed copy of itself.
You can use a higher-frequency oscillator, like a MEMS or SAW oscillator, or an overtone crystal. A DLL can create multiplied or multi-phase clocks too.
But for general-purpose multiplication, the PLL is the answer.

And I'd add that a faster clock isn't free: dynamic power goes up linearly with frequency, timing margins shrink, and the PLL adds jitter, so you only go as fast as the logic and the power budget allow."
